comp-01-c2.text: Cristopher Moore (2019). Automata, languages, and grammars (lecture notes). arXiv:1907.12713.
comp-01-c2.quote: Any NFA can be simulated by a DFA that accepts the same language.
comp-01-c2.claim: Every NFA can be converted to an equivalent DFA using the subset construction.

comp-01-c2.text: Tal Malkin (2018). DFA can be exponentially larger than equivalent NFA (COMS W3261 notes). Columbia University, Department of Computer Science.
comp-01-c2.quote: The theorem shows that sometimes the transformation from an NFA to an equivalent DFA necessitates an exponential blow up in the number of states.
comp-01-c2.claim: The DFA may need exponentially more states, since an NFA with n states might need up to 2^n DFA states, but it recognizes exactly the same language.

comp-01-c3.text: Sariel Har-Peled and Madhusudan Parthasarathy (2009). CS 373: Theory of Computation, Lecture 9: Proving non-regularity. University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign.
comp-01-c3.quote: Intuitively, L can not be regular, because we have to remember how many a’s we have seen before reading the b’s, and this can not be done with a finite number of states.
comp-01-c3.claim: It isn't regular, because recognizing it means counting how many a's you've seen and matching that count with b's.

comp-09-c2.text: Neil Immerman (2004). Computability and Complexity. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
comp-09-c2.quote: In fact, a set is recursive iff it is r.e. and co-r.e.
comp-09-c2.claim: A language is decidable exactly when it is both RE and co-RE: run the two half-machines side by side, and one of them must eventually answer.

comp-09-c2.text: The bbchallenge Collaboration (2025). Determination of the fifth Busy Beaver value. arXiv.
comp-09-c2.quote: historically introduced by Tibor Radó in 1962 as one of the simplest examples of an uncomputable function
comp-09-c2.claim: The Busy Beaver function (Tibor Radó, 1962) asks for the longest any halting n-state machine can run, and it eventually outgrows every computable function.

comp-09-c2.text: The bbchallenge Collaboration (2024). The Busy Beaver Challenge. bbchallenge.org.
comp-09-c2.quote: We have reached our goal of proving "BB(5) = 47,176,870"
comp-09-c2.claim: Its fifth value, 47,176,870 steps, was settled only in 2024 by the online Busy Beaver Challenge collaboration, with the proof checked in the Coq proof assistant.

comp-09-c2.text: Adam Yedidia, Scott Aaronson (2016). A Relatively Small Turing Machine Whose Behavior Is Independent of Set Theory. arXiv.
comp-09-c2.quote: presenting an explicit description of a 7,910-state Turing machine Z with 1 tape and a 2-symbol alphabet that cannot be proved to run forever in ZFC (even though it presumably does), assuming ZFC is consistent
comp-09-c2.claim: Later values outrun mathematics itself: in 2016 Adam Yedidia and Scott Aaronson built a 7,910-state machine whose halting can be neither proved nor disproved from the standard ZFC axioms of set theory.

comp-09-c3.text: Walter Dean (2015). Computational Complexity Theory. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
comp-09-c3.quote: This paper is also the origin of the so-called Hierarchy Theorems (see Section 3.2) which demonstrate that a sufficiently large increase in the time or space bound for a Turing machine computation allows more problems to be decided.
comp-09-c3.claim: The hierarchy theorems (Juris Hartmanis, Richard Stearns and Philip Lewis, 1965) prove that more of the same resource buys strictly more power, so P ≠ EXPTIME and NL ≠ PSPACE.

comp-09-c3.text: Walter Dean (2015). Computational Complexity Theory. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
comp-09-c3.quote: suggesting that non-determinism is computationally less powerful with respect to space than it appears to be with respect to time

comp-09-c3.text: Walter J. Savitch (1970). Relationships between nondeterministic and deterministic tape complexities. Journal of Computer and System Sciences.
comp-09-c3.quote: A nondeterministic L(n)-tape bounded Turing machine can be simulated by a deterministic [L(n)]^2-tape bounded Turing machine
comp-09-c3.claim: Savitch's theorem (1970) shows a deterministic machine can simulate a guessing one with only quadratically more memory, so NPSPACE = PSPACE.

comp-09-c3.text: Peter W. Shor (1995). Polynomial-Time Algorithms for Prime Factorization and Discrete Logarithms on a Quantum Computer. arXiv.
comp-09-c3.quote: This paper considers factoring integers and finding discrete logarithms, two problems which are generally thought to be hard on a classical computer and have been used as the basis of several proposed cryptosystems. Efficient randomized algorithms are given for these two problems on a hypothetical quantum computer.

comp-09-c3.text: Adi Shamir (1992). IP = PSPACE. Journal of the ACM.
comp-09-c3.claim: Adi Shamir proved in 1992 that IP = PSPACE.

comp-09-c4.text: Omer Reingold (2008). Undirected connectivity in log-space. Journal of the ACM.
comp-09-c4.claim: Omer Reingold showed in 2005 that the undirected version is in L.

comp-09-c4.text: Richard E. Ladner (1975). The circuit value problem is log space complete for P. ACM SIGACT News.
comp-09-c4.quote: The circuit value problem is log space complete for P

comp-09-c4.text: Aviezri S. Fraenkel, David Lichtenstein (1981). Computing a perfect strategy for n × n chess requires time exponential in n. Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A.
comp-09-c4.quote: Computing a perfect strategy for n × n chess requires time exponential in n
comp-09-c4.claim: chess generalized to n×n boards (Aviezri Fraenkel and David Lichtenstein, 1981)

comp-09-c4.text: OpenAI (2026). The Exponential Time Hypothesis is False. OpenAI Math Release preprint.
comp-09-c4.quote: We give a deterministic algorithm for exactly counting the satisfying assignments of an arbitrary k-CNF formula.
comp-09-c4.claim: On 26 October 2026, OpenAI released a preprint, which it says its AI model produced, claiming a deterministic algorithm that counts the solutions of any k-SAT formula in time about \(2^{n/\sqrt{\log n}}\) using polynomial space.

comp-09-c4.text: OpenAI (2026). The Exponential Time Hypothesis is False. OpenAI Math Release preprint.
comp-09-c4.quote: In this paper, we refute ETH by giving, for every fixed k ⩾ 2, a deterministic algorithm that counts the satisfying assignments of a k-CNF in subexponential time
comp-09-c4.claim: That is still super-polynomial, so P vs NP is untouched, but it is sub-exponential, which would make ETH and its stronger cousin SETH false.

comp-09-c4.text: Ana Maria Constantin (2026). OpenAI says its AI model has disproved the Exponential Time Hypothesis. TNW.
comp-09-c4.quote: A group led by Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi of UC San Diego and Ryan Williams of MIT will check and explain the result.
comp-09-c4.claim: A version with a slightly weaker bound has been checked in the Lean proof assistant, and Impagliazzo, Paturi and Ryan Williams are examining the paper; as of late October 2026 it has not been peer reviewed.

comp-09-c5.text: Neil Immerman (2004). Computability and Complexity. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
comp-09-c5.quote: a property is in NP iff it is expressible in second-order existential logic [Fagin, 1974]
comp-09-c5.claim: Ronald Fagin proved in 1974 that NP is exactly what existential second-order logic can express, with no machines mentioned at all, and Neil Immerman and Moshe Vardi characterized P on ordered structures as first-order logic plus a fixed-point operator.

comp-09-c1.text: David Matuszek (1996). The Chomsky Hierarchy. CSC 4170 lecture notes.
comp-09-c1.quote: The Chomsky hierarchy, as originally defined by Noam Chomsky, comprises four types of languages and their associated grammars and machines.
comp-09-c1.claim: In papers from 1956 and 1959 the linguist Noam Chomsky arranged the matching grammars into a single ladder, and each rung of grammar lines up exactly with a rung of machine.

comp-09-c1.text: David Matuszek (1996). The Chomsky Hierarchy. CSC 4170 lecture notes.
comp-09-c1.quote: These languages form a strict hierarchy

comp-09-c1.text: David Matuszek (1996). Extending the Chomsky Hierarchy. CSC 4170 lecture notes.
comp-09-c1.quote: deterministic pushdown automata were less powerful than nondeterministic pushdown automata
comp-09-c1.claim: Deterministic pushdown automata are strictly weaker than nondeterministic ones (even-length palindromes need the guess "this is the middle"), which is why practical parsers stick to deterministic grammars such as LR(k).
